rows.searchedFor: if I want the whole company to start using some new app, how do I get that approved?
rows.answer:
The handbook says you start by trying the tool in a low-risk context.[1] That means a context where it is easily replaced and doesn't involve sensitive data, and if you're unsure what information can be shared, check with #legal first.[2]

Next steps:
- Open a pull request in Company Internal and, at the same time, open an issue describing why we should adopt the tool.[3] Think about the impact on the whole company, not just your team or use case.[4]
- Your proposal should consider the "what to think about" guidelines, which are not a rigid checklist; the aim is a holistic review of risks against benefits.[5] Many proposals will not make it past this stage, and the handbook says that's good.[6]

If the decision is to adopt it:
- The person proposing the tool is responsible for coordinating the next steps.[7]
- You negotiate business terms with the vendor, such as cost, licenses or usage limits, contract length, and implementation or onboarding details.[8]
- As soon as it looks like you'll move forward, post in #legal to say a decision has been made, business terms are being negotiated, and contract documents will be shared shortly.[9]
- Once documents are available, send them to #legal in an editable format such as .docx.[10]
- Legal review usually takes a few business days, and negotiations can take longer, so involve legal early and tell them ahead of time if you have a deadline.[11]
- If the vendor qualifies as a subprocessor, the review will usually be more involved.[12]
- The tool can be used in production once legal review is complete, contracts are finalized and signed, and any required subprocessor notice period has passed.[13]

This process doesn't apply to "cheap decisions" that are easily completed or reversed, or that only affect your own work. For those, follow the software section of the spending money page.[14]

rows.searchedFor: if my PR touches a github actions workflow, does it need a special reviewer?
rows.answer:
Great care should be taken when writing or modifying a GitHub Actions workflow, because Actions can access (and exfiltrate) secrets scoped to the repo.[1]

- Workflows are scanned with Semgrep and CodeQL for common misconfigurations.[1]
- In the Shai-Hulud incident, a workflow change was flagged by a static analysis tool before merge, but the alert was dismissed because the team mistakenly thought the usage was safe.[2]
- If you need help setting up a new GitHub App for an Action, you can send a message in #team-security.[3]

rows.searchedFor: is there a rubric or list of criteria I need to hit to move up here?
rows.answer:
The handbook says there is no checklist or formal framework: it describes a checklist or formal career progression framework as self-interested by nature, so it creates the wrong incentives, and says the benefits of frameworks only start to outweigh their drawbacks when you need to coordinate 100s of people.[1]

What it does say about progressing:
- The best way to progress is to understand your team's and PostHog's objectives, then ship fast towards them, give and receive direct feedback, and fix problems when you see them.[2]
- The inputs that lead to progression are caring about your work, your team, and your users. The handbook says that if you consistently care, PostHog will progress you.[3]
- If the company is succeeding, it is easy to justify, and to afford, pay rises where people are performing very well.[4]
- It also says that getting a manager to progress you isn't the route, because that gives too much power to managers, and that your motivation to progress has to be intrinsic.[5]
- There is no wide range of fancy titles, because the aim is for people to be as equal as possible.[6]

rows.searchedFor: a customer runs posthog inside their browser extension and their bill is way higher than it should be, how do they fix it?
rows.answer:
The handbook's Wildfire Systems case study gives the fix. Persist the UUID manually using chrome.storage.local, and pass it during posthog.init() with bootstrap.distinctID.[1] This matters because local storage is isolated per context, so the SDK couldn't persist the ID and created a new anonymous ID on each wake cycle.[2]

The other recommendations for extension developers are:

- Only call identify() if the ID has changed.[3] The cause was that each new ID triggered a comparison to the persisted UUID, and since they always differed, identify() was called each time.[4]
- Reduce /flags usage by using bootstrap.featureFlags and disabling polling if needed.[5] This helps because every call to identify() refreshed feature flags[6], and /flags requests were billed even when quota-limited.[7]
- Monitor proactively with the "My PostHog Billable Usage" dashboard.[8]
- Customers should be aware that extensions require manual handling.[9]

One caveat: raising the billing limit mid-cycle did not retroactively unlock flags; only new requests after the monthly reset were allowed.[10]

rows.searchedFor: how do tickets get divvied up on the support team? does everyone work every product?
rows.answer:
Not entirely: all technical support engineers work on some shared areas, and beyond that SMEs own specific product groups, with one person from EU and one from NA per group for timezone coverage.[1][2]

- Everyone works on Analytics products, since they make up the highest proportion of tickets, and on unclassified tickets, which should be updated with the correct product group where possible.[3]
- The SME product groups listed are Flags, Data, Replay, Observability + AI & client libraries, and Analytics.[4][5][6][7][8]
- Each SME has a dedicated Zendesk view with tickets from their own product groups plus the shared groups (analytics and unclassified).[9][10] These views also show tickets assigned to other team members, so you can jump in if you know something or see someone stuck.[11]
- SMEs start with their SME views, then move to the Technical support shared view, which has all tickets the technical support team is responsible for.[12] They aren't locked into only their SME products: if caught up, they help with the shared queue, and if swamped, they can ask for help with their SME queue.[13]
- New support engineers usually spend their first few weeks focused just on product and web analytics tickets.[14]
- When picking tickets, avoid cherry-picking and take the one closest to breaching response targets.[15] For unassigned tickets, check whether someone else is already viewing a ticket to avoid duplicate work.[16]

rows.searchedFor: what's the cutoff for a new lead to get worked by sales instead of just going self-serve?
rows.answer:
The handbook's cutoff is about $20k: if a lead will be too small (<$20k) for the sales-led process and you can't get the information from them, you should route them to self-serve.[1] When qualifying, you consider company size, revenue, and funding, i.e. whether they will pay >$20k for PostHog.[2]

The handbook also lists points to consider when deciding whether to mark a lead self-serve:
- If their usage volume is around 5 million monthly events and 100,000 recordings, they should be hands-on.[3]
- If they want an annual commitment, keep them in the hands-on pipeline.[4]
- If they need help with a guided evaluation and their potential value is high enough, create a Slack Connect channel and keep them in the hands-on pipeline.[4]
- If none of these apply, move them to self-serve.[5]

rows.searchedFor: I want to interview one of our customers for a story on the website, anyone I should check with before I email them?
rows.answer:
Yes, before reaching out, search for the company in Vitally; if they already have an assigned Account Executive or CSM, give that person a heads-up, since they might already be working on something with the customer or have extra context on what to ask.[1] If no one is assigned in Vitally, you're clear to reach out directly.[2]

Also, some customers have a dedicated Slack channel, which is usually the fastest way to coordinate; otherwise, send an email.[3]

rows.searchedFor: Do we give customers anything for participating in an interview for a story on the website?
rows.answer:
Yes, the handbook says once the case study is merged and live on the website, the last step is to send a merch credit to the participants as a thank you.[1] It also says PostHog will typically thank customers who participate in case studies and collab content by sending them a merch voucher.[2]

Discounts are not part of this. PostHog doesn't offer additional discounts in exchange for a case study, as paying for case studies can devalue them.[3]

rows.answer:
- The benchmark is Culture Amp's "new tech" companies with fewer than 200 people.[1]

- A summary of results is reported in an Issue following a template, and the latest survey results are linked from the handbook.[2]
